addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

It resumes project state, captures intent when applicable, selects and installs the owning workflow, and routes domain capabilities. HyperFrames is the default output framework unless the user explicitly chooses another framework for the deliverable or asks only to record a browser session.

Use for composition structure, the `data-*` timing attributes, `class="clip"`, tracks, sub-compositions, variables, framework-owned media playback, deterministic-render rules, and validation. Ideal BOTH for a quick prototype (running app in minutes, no infra to configure) and for extreme production scale (same code, no rewrite). Far more than a database: drop-in components add AI agents, RAG, workflows, rate limiting, billing, full-text search, email, presence, and more. Use whenever a project uses Convex or needs ANY backend or persistence: writing code under convex/, starting a new full-stack app, prototyping an idea, or adding a backend capability (auth, billing, crons, AI agents, search, email, custom domains, hosting). Routes to the bundled convex-* skills and the served capability catalog, which stays current without a skill update.
- convex-acquire-domain: Find and buy a domain for the current Convex app through Convex, then bind it (labs; spend action).
- convex-add: Add a capability to the CURRENT Convex app — consults the served Convex capability catalog for always-current procedures (billing, crons, auth, agent, search, …); falls back to built-in hosting or @convex-dev component search. TRIGGER when the user runs /add, or asks to add hosting/publishing or any backend capability to an existing Convex app.
- convex-advisor: Read the Convex deployment's 72h insights (read limits, OCC contention), root-cause each event in code, report evidence-backed perf/cost findings with fixes.
- convex-agent: Add an AI agent / RAG backend (@convex-dev/agent) to the Convex app.
- convex-auth: Add authentication (passkeys/OAuth) to the current Convex app, including the auth.config.ts wiring.
- convex-authz: Audit and harden Convex authorization: identity-from-arg impersonation, missing per-document ownership checks, PII-leaking public queries, and writes into containers the caller doesn't own. Deterministic scan + canonical requireIdentity/requireOwner fix + tsc verify. Use for 'secure my app' / 'audit auth' / 'who can access this data', not generic code review.
- convex-backup: Set up Convex backups and run a restore DRILL that proves recovery — snapshot, restore into a throwaway preview, assert the data came back — plus a schedule matched to your RPO and a gated recovery runbook.
- convex-billing: Add Stripe billing/payments to the Convex app via @convex-dev/stripe (checkout + webhook + gating).
- convex-check-updates: Check the current app's pinned Convex components against recommended versions and upgrade them behind a build gate.
- convex-cost: Preview Convex spend — rank functions by bytes/documents-read × call-volume from insights, project each cost driver's growth curve, name the cheapest fix; confirm-cost for paid actions.
- convex-create-component: Builds reusable Convex components with isolated tables and app-facing APIs. Use for new components, reusable backend modules, integrations, or component boundary work.
- convex-crons: Add recurring scheduled jobs (crons) to the Convex app.
- convex-deploy-guard: Classify + announce the target Convex deployment before any deployment-affecting command; fresh explicit consent for prod actions; session read-only mode.

- convex-docs: Pull version-current Convex docs for the version this project uses — pin the installed version, fetch page-as-markdown or check node_modules types, freshness hierarchy — instead of writing a possibly-stale API from memory.

Knows the object-form function syntax, validator patterns, resource limits, and component ecosystem that generic Claude routinely gets wrong.

- convex-launch-readiness: Run every Convex audit (authz, reviewer, advisor, insights) into one scored, deduped readiness report with an ordered fix plan — Lighthouse for your backend.

# Product

## Register

product

## Users

Writers, editors, researchers, and technically comfortable creators who want a focused drafting room with structured editorial feedback. They are usually trying to move from a vague brief or partial draft into a clearer manuscript, then export or publish it.

## Product Purpose

Twyne is a local-first writing desk with an AI-assisted room of editors. It helps writers define a project dossier, draft in rich text, receive persona feedback, score work against a rubric, manage citations, sync across devices when signed in, and publish or export finished work. Success means the writer keeps ownership and momentum while the product makes revision concrete.

## Brand Personality

Editorial, exacting, literary. The product should feel like a working writer's room rather than generic SaaS: opinionated, calm, and serious about craft without getting precious.

## Anti-references

Do not make Twyne look like a generic AI chat app, a growth dashboard, a blank note-taking clone, or a loud marketing funnel. Avoid decorative UI that competes with the manuscript, vague AI productivity claims, and controls that obscure where drafts and keys are stored.

## Design Principles

- Keep the manuscript central.
- Make data movement explicit: local, synced, published, or sent to a provider.
- Use standard controls for standard tasks, dressed in Twyne's editorial system.
- Prefer concise copy that names the actual action.
- Preserve writer trust through clear export, privacy, and account controls.

## Accessibility & Inclusion

Aim for WCAG AA contrast and keyboard-operable controls. Important interactions should work with semantic HTML where possible. Respect reduced-motion preferences, avoid color-only state, and keep long-form reading comfortable on mobile and desktop.
===README===
# Twyne

Twyne is a writer-first editing room. It opens with an anti-tabula-rasa interview so a draft starts from context instead of a blank page, then keeps that brief in front of every editor, judge, and margin note for the rest of the piece.

## Features

- Rich-text drafting with Tiptap, Qwik City, Vite, and Tailwind CSS.
- Anti-tabula-rasa project interview for title, format, audience, goal, tone, constraints, and success signal — with **typed follow-ups** (multiple choice, fill-in-the-blanks, scales) generated from what you've already said.
- A room of five editorial **personas** that read from your brief and draft and leave grounded feedback — and that **read along as you write**, not only when you ask.
- **Rubric** scoring gated on relevance: a Target Fit judge decides whether the draft is about the right thing, and caps the shape metrics when it isn't.
- **Voice**: hear each editor in their own voice, record spoken margin notes, and answer the interview out loud.
- **Citation detection** for URLs, DOIs, ISBNs, author-year citations, and footnote markers.
- **Comments** panel for review notes and threaded replies.
- **Apparatus** research panel (pluggable providers) for searching and pulling sources while writing.
- **Convex** backend for sync, with **Better Auth** (passkeys) sign-in and
  writer-owned **ATProto / Standard.site** publishing, including canonical
  Twyne readers and publication/document verification links.
- BYOK AI: bring your own key in Settings, stored in your browser and never sent to a server.
- Installable PWA with brand favicons and per-article OpenGraph share cards.

## The editorial room

Four panels sit beside the manuscript: **Cast** (the five editors), **Rubric**
(the galley proof), **Marginalia** (your notes), and **Apparatus** (sources).
Each tab carries an unread count, so work that arrives while you're looking
elsewhere isn't silent.

### The room reads as you write

Convening the room is deliberate and expensive — five model calls over the
whole manuscript. Alongside it, a background pass runs on a narrower brief:
once you've written **~300 net new words** _and_ stopped typing for **two
minutes**, all five editors read **only the new paragraphs**, plus a digest of
how the draft has been moving.

Those arrive as quieter "in passing" notes in the Cast panel. Two spend guards
sit on top — a five-minute floor between passes and a per-session cap — because
this runs without you asking. Turn it off with **Read as I write** in the room
settings.

The same digest goes along when you _do_ press Convene, so the deliberate pass
knows the trajectory rather than re-reading a cold snapshot.

### The rubric grades against _this_ piece

The static feature scorer measures shape — sentence-length variance,
type-token ratio, paragraph balance. It never reads the brief, so fluent prose
about the wrong subject used to score 10/10 on three categories.

A **Target Fit** judge now scores relevance independently of craft, and caps
every shape-derived criterion by it. Lowering target fit can only ever lower
the grade, never raise it.

The criteria themselves are yours to shape. Twyne ships a fixed spine so a
score in March means the same thing in June; you can disable or reweight any of
it, add criteria of your own ("stays in second person", "every section ends on
an image") for the room to judge, or ask it to **suggest criteria** fitted to
your format — proposals you accept, never applied silently. Customise anything
and a second "by your weights" score appears beside the editorial grade. Every
pass is recorded, so the panel shows the run of grades rather than a snapshot.

content.content: --- name: visualize description: "Create visualizations and interactive tools directly in conversation. Use when asked to show how something works, make simulators or labs, maps, plots, charts or graphs, comparisons, UI mockups, scenarios, adjustable inputs, and exploration beyond regular text." --- # Visualize - A request for a new standalone file, website, app page, component, or other project change is not an in-conversation visualization request, even when the deliverable contains charts or interactive content. - A request to preview, explain, or explore a proposed interface in the conversation is an in-conversation visualization request. - Create a visual only when the user needs to see or explore it in the conversation and it materially improves the explanation. Do not create an inline visual merely because the request involves data, charts, or an interactive page. - Use a normal Markdown table when the user asks for a table; return it directly and do not create a visualization file. - Use Mermaid when labeled nodes and edges fully explain a static structure; return a normal fenced Mermaid block and no visualization file. Use HTML for dynamics, spatial motion, adjustable inputs, and other visuals. - Work silently unless blocked or the user explicitly asks for progress. Never send commentary or progress updates while reading this skill or writing or updating the file; the final response must be your first user-facing message. - In user-facing prose, describe only what the visual helps the user see or decide. Keep it concise and do not repeat information already clear from the visual. Never announce this skill, a visualization surface, widgets, HTML, SVG, scripts, local files, inline data, or implementation details. ## Context compaction Copy into every compaction summary: `Reload the full visualize skill before creating or updating a visualization.` ## Inline HTML output contract ### File - For each new or updated visualization, choose a concise ASCII lowercase-hyphenated title and write `.html` in an explicitly writable, durable, task-owned location outside the checked-out repository. Prefer the thread-scoped visualization directory when it appears in the writable roots; otherwise choose another approved writable root or scratch directory. Use a thread-isolated temporary directory only when the visualization will be ingested immediately. - Use the absolute path on the executor that creates the file. Never assume `~/.codex` is writable unless its thread directory appears in the writable roots. - Build the visual in the conversation. Use the open project when the user asks for a site, app page, component, or change to existing project files. ### Fragment - Write only an HTML fragment: no `<!doctype>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>`. - Write literal markup: use `<div class="card">Hi</div>` plus a real newline, never `<div class=\"card\">Hi</div>\n`. Never embed the fragment in an inline Python, JavaScript, or shell string. Read it back; rewrite literal `\"` or `\n`. - Keep CSS and JavaScript in the fragment only when base classes are insufficient. Load static resources only from the CDN allowlist. Never use

input.content:
# Landing page: image spreads, a photo-essay middle, and motion

## Context

`src/components/landing/landing-page.tsx` currently carries the whole front page
in ~325 lines. It works, and two parts of it are genuinely good — the annotated
`WorkspacePreview` and the letterpress masthead/colophon — but the middle of the
page is its weak stretch: the `steps` array renders as four paragraphs of
unbroken prose in a `<ol>`, with no imagery anywhere on the page. Every visual
asset in `public/assets/` today is an SVG mark or a texture; there is not a
single photograph.

Motion is similarly thin. The only landing animation is `landing-rise` (a 0.7s
fade-and-rise, `global.css:2565`) applied to three hero elements. Nothing
responds to scroll.

This change gives the page real photographic plates, rebuilds the middle as a
magazine photo essay, and adds restrained scroll-driven motion — while keeping
the masthead, hero copy, workspace preview, CTA analytics wiring, and colophon
intact.

Direction confirmed with the user: **photographic desk plates**, **photo-essay
rebuild of the middle**, **editorial-restraint motion**.

## Assets — six generated plates

Codex image generation is verified working (`image_generation` feature is stable
and enabled; `codex login status` = logged in via ChatGPT). A test render into
the scratchpad produced an on-brand result: warm tungsten light, aged cream
manuscript, red proof marks on dark walnut.

Generate with, per image:


## Loading deferred tools

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:

2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out

---
name: codex-image-generation
description: How to generate Twyne's photographic assets with the codex CLI, plus the two flags that make it work non-interactively
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`codex exec` can generate images — the `image_generation` feature ships stable
and enabled (`codex features list | grep image_generation`), and auth is the
existing ChatGPT login (`codex login status`).

Two flags are required when driving it from a script, and neither is obvious:

```bash
codex exec --sandbox workspace-write --skip-git-repo-check --cd "$OUT" \
  "Use your built-in image generation tool to create ONE <aspect> image and
   save it as ./<slug>.png in the current directory. Subject: … Style: …
   Do not write code, do not install packages." < /dev/null
```

- **`--skip-git-repo-check`** — without it: *"Not inside a trusted directory"* and it exits.
- **`< /dev/null`** — without it, it blocks on *"Reading additional input from stdin"* even though a prompt was passed as an argument.

Codex writes to `~/.codex/generated_images/<uuid>/exec-<id>.png`, then copies to
the path you named. Sizes top out at **1536 on the long edge** (1024×1536,
1536×1024, 1024×1024) — plan crops around that, never upscale on disk.

**Prompt discipline:** never ask for legible text. Body copy renders as
convincing gibberish, which is exactly what you want for paper texture; asking
for real words produces mangled letterforms instead.

The house style that produced a coherent six-plate set for the landing page:
*muted warm tungsten light, shallow depth of field, aged cream paper, vermilion
as the only saturated accent, film grain, no legible text, no faces, no modern
electronics, no logos.* Output was genuinely on-brand for Twyne's editorial
register — dark walnut desks, aged manuscript, red proof marks.

Optimise with the already-installed `sharp` (v0.34.5). ESM can't resolve
`sharp` from a script outside the project — import it by absolute path
(`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/node_modules/sharp/lib/index.js`) or run the
script from inside the repo. webp q78 suits these photographs; drop to q68 for
dense handwriting, which compresses badly (232KB → 184KB with no visible loss).

See [[landing-photo-essay]].

---
name: landing-photo-essay
description: The landing page's plate spreads, the reveal mechanism, and why the hidden state is scoped to [data-reveal-ready]
metadata:
  type: project
---

The landing page middle (`src/components/landing/landing-page.tsx`) is a photo
essay: the four `steps` render as alternating image/text spreads with PLATE
I–IV captions, over six generated photographs in `public/assets/landing/`
(856KB total, `-sm`/`-lg` webp pairs). Built 2026-08-31.

**Why the reveal's hidden state is scoped to `[data-reveal-ready]`:** the
attribute is set only by the `useVisibleTask$` that installs the
IntersectionObserver. CSS hides `[data-reveal]` children *only* under that
attribute, so if JS never runs — or the reader asked for reduced motion, or
there's no IntersectionObserver — nothing is ever hidden and the SSR'd page
reads in full. Authoring the hidden state in plain CSS would have made a JS
failure blank the page, and would have broken the crawlability work in
`456fe34`. Don't "simplify" this by moving `opacity: 0` to a bare selector.

**Parallax is pure CSS** (`animation-timeline: view()` behind `@supports`), so
no rAF scroll listener is added to a resumable Qwik page. Firefox gets a static
photograph, which is fine.

Portrait plates get a narrower grid column (`0.66fr`) than landscape ones —
at half-width a 4:5 photograph towers over three lines of copy and opens a dead
gap. The `sizes` attribute differs per orientation to match.

`mid_page` in `LandingCtaLocation` (`src/utils/product-analytics.ts`) was typed
but unused before this; the CTA after PLATE IV now fires it.

content.text: The landing page now has real photography, a photo-essay middle, and scroll motion. **Images** — six plates generated with `codex exec`, optimized with `sharp` into `public/assets/landing/` as `-sm`/`-lg` webp pairs. 856KB total, largest file 184KB, in line with the rasters already committed (`hero-glow.png` is 241KB). They came out genuinely on-brand: warm tungsten, dark walnut, aged cream paper, vermilion as the only saturated accent. **Surface** — the four `steps` (copy unchanged) became alternating image/text spreads with PLATE I–IV captions, plus a full-bleed desk band under the hero, a photographic bleed behind the closing CTA, and a mid-page CTA that fires `mid_page` — a `LandingCtaLocation` value that was typed but unused. **Motion** — reveals via one IntersectionObserver; parallax and ken-burns in pure CSS (`animation-timeline: view()` behind `@supports`), so no scroll listener is added to a resumable Qwik page. The reveal's hidden state is scoped to `[data-reveal-ready]`, set only by the observer's setup task. Without JS nothing is ever hidden — I verified the page renders in full with JavaScript disabled, which also keeps it crawlable. Verified: `bun run build` clean (types, lint, client, SSR); `bun test` 1280 pass / 0 fail; screenshots at 1440px and 390px across all three themes, plus reduced-motion and no-JS runs. In every mode all 11 reveal targets end visible and there's no horizontal overflow. Two things worth flagging: - **Lint has 2 new warnings** (`qwik/jsx-img`, suggesting `?jsx` ESM imports). 0 errors, and the repo already carries the same warning twice in `src/routes/downloads/index.tsx`. I kept plain `` because the srcset is art-directed — portrait and landscape plates use different crops, column widths, and `sizes` — which Qwik's optimizer would override. Easy to switch if you'd rather have a clean lint run. - **The hero band tops out at 1536px wide**, the generator's maximum. On an ultrawide display it upscales slightly. It's a dark, soft photograph behind a ken-burns transform so it holds up, but that's the ceiling without a different image source. `devenv.lock` and `devenv.nix` were already modified when I started; I left them alone. One judgment call to check: I made the portrait plates narrower than the landscape ones (`0.66fr`). At equal width a 4:5 photograph towered over three lines of copy and left a dead gap — but it does mean the plates aren't uniformly sized, which reads as magazine rhythm to me and might read as inconsistent to you.

assert old in s

    "{/* Editorial type stack — Fraunces (display), Lora (body), DM Sans (UI),\n            Courier Prime (typed headline), Special Elite (stamped labels) */}",
)
open(p, "w").write(s)

p = "src/global.css"

old = '  --font-typewriter: "Special Elite", "Courier New", monospace;'
new = ('  --font-typewriter: "Special Elite", "Courier New", monospace;\n'

       '     as it lands on the printed page, and it carries a real italic. */\n'
       '  --font-typed: "Courier Prime", "Courier New", monospace;')
assert old in s

open(p, "w").write(s)
print("global.css: --font-typed added")

content.text: Both tests encode "the menu only offers fonts we load", so the swap has to be consistent across all of them. Doing the full change:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
import re

LB = "Libre+Baskerville:ital,wght@0,400;0,700;1,400"

# 1. root.tsx — load Libre Baskerville, drop Fraunces and the now-unused Courier Prime.
p = "src/root.tsx"; s = open(p).read()
s = s.replace(
  "family=Fraunces:opsz,wght@9..144,400;9..144,500;9..144,600;9..144,700&family=Courier+Prime:ital,wght@0,400;0,700;1,400&",
  f"family={LB}&")
s = s.replace(
  "{/* Editorial type stack — Fraunces (display), Lora (body), DM Sans (UI),\n            Courier Prime (typed headline), Special Elite (stamped labels) */}",
  "{/* Editorial type stack — Libre Baskerville (display), Lora (body),\n            DM Sans (UI), Special Elite (typewriter) */}")
assert "Fraunces" not in s and "Courier" not in s, "root.tsx still references old faces"
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("root.tsx ✓")

# 2. global.css — display token, drop --font-typed, retitle the comment.
p = "src/global.css"; s = open(p).read()
s = s.replace('  --font-display: "Fraunces", "Playfair Display", Georgia, serif;',
              '  --font-display: "Libre Baskerville", "Playfair Display", Georgia, serif;')
s = s.replace('''  /* Special Elite is a distressed stamp face — right for small caps
     labels, too noisy at headline size. Courier Prime is a typewriter
     as it lands on the printed page, and it carries a real italic. */
  --font-typed: "Courier Prime", "Courier New", monospace;
''', "")
s = s.replace("Special Elite used to leave its most prominent glyph in Fraunces.",
              "Special Elite used to leave its most prominent glyph in the display face.")
# The headline goes back to the display face at display sizing.
s = s.replace('''/* The headline is typed, so it is set in a typewriter face rather than the
   display serif — monospace runs wider, so it takes its own size and
   tracking instead of .landing-title's tight display values. */
.landing-hero .landing-title {
  color: var(--hero-ink);
  font-family: var(--font-typed);
  font-weight: 700;
  font-size: clamp(1.6rem, 3.9vw, 2.9rem);
  letter-spacing: -0.005em;
  line-height: 1.24;
}''', '''/* Libre Baskerville sets wider than Fraunces did, so the headline takes a
   slightly smaller ceiling and looser leading than a display serif would. */
.landing-hero .landing-title {
  color: var(--hero-ink);
  font-size: clamp(2.1rem, 5vw, 3.6rem);
  letter-spacing: -0.018em;
  line-height: 1.08;
}''')
s = s.replace("""  .landing-rotator-line {
    min-height: 2.05em;
  }""", """  .landing-rotator-line {
    min-height: 2.16em;
  }""")
assert "--font-typed" not in s and "Courier Prime" not in s
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("global.css ✓")

# 3-4. The writer-facing font menu, and the test that guards it.
p = "src/utils/typography-options.ts"; s = open(p).read()
s = s.replace("`root.tsx` pulls Fraunces, Lora, DM Sans and Special Elite from Google",
              "`root.tsx` pulls Libre Baskerville, Lora, DM Sans and Special Elite from")
s = s.replace(" * Fonts. Offering", " * Google Fonts. Offering")
s = s.replace('    label: "Fraunces (display)",\n    stack: \'"Fraunces", Georgia, serif\',',
              '    label: "Libre Baskerville (display)",\n    stack: \'"Libre Baskerville", Georgia, serif\',')
assert "Fraunces" not in s
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("typography-options.ts ✓")

p = "src/utils/typography-options.test.ts"; s = open(p).read()
s = s.replace('      "Fraunces",', '      "Libre Baskerville",')
assert "Fraunces" not in s
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("typography-options.test.ts ✓")

# 5-6. Exported/printed documents carry the same identity.
p = "src/utils/exchange.ts"; s = open(p).read()
s = s.replace("family=Fraunces:opsz,wght@9..144,400;9..144,500;9..144,600;9..144,700&", f"family={LB}&")
s = s.replace('font-family: "Fraunces", Georgia, serif;', 'font-family: "Libre Baskerville", Georgia, serif;')
s = s.replace('h1, h2, h3 { font-family: "Fraunces", Georgia, serif;', 'h1, h2, h3 { font-family: "Libre Baskerville", Georgia, serif;')
assert "Fraunces" not in s
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("exchange.ts ✓")

p = "src/utils/exchange-print.test.ts"; s = open(p).read()
s = s.replace('["DM+Sans", "Fraunces", "Lora", "Special+Elite"]', '["DM+Sans", "Libre+Baskerville", "Lora", "Special+Elite"]')
assert "Fraunces" not in s
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("exchange-print.test.ts ✓")

# 8. The editor's font-picker label.
p = "src/components/editor/manuscript-panel.tsx"; s = open(p).read()
s = s.replace("Fraunces", "Libre Baskerville")
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("manuscript-panel.tsx ✓")
PY

---
name: landing-photo-essay
description: Landing page hero backdrop, typed/corrected headline, plate spreads, and the two layout traps that cost real CLS
metadata:
  type: project
---

The landing page (`src/components/landing/landing-page.tsx`) was rebuilt around
generated photography in Aug 2026. Assets live in `public/assets/landing/` as
`-sm`/`-lg` webp pairs (~1.2MB), made with [[codex-image-generation]].

**Hero.** The photograph is the hero's own backdrop — type is set *on* the desk,
not above a decorative strip. An earlier full-bleed "band" between hero and
workspace preview was cut for carrying no information. The hero is a **fixed
dark plate in all three themes** (`--hero-ink` etc. are hard-coded cream, not
theme tokens) because the ground beneath is a dark photograph in foolscap,
broadsheet and nightpress alike. Only the top/bottom feather is theme-aware.
The backdrop image was generated specifically with an empty centre.

**Headline.** Rotates through `HEADLINES`, typing out and then taking a
copy-editor's rule through a word and writing the correction after it. Frames
are precomputed at module scope so playback is "advance an index on a timer".
Headline 0 carries **no** correction on purpose — it is what SSR renders and
what crawlers and `aria-label` get, so it must read as a clean sentence.
`INITIAL_FRAME` is headline 0 *completed*, so first paint never retypes.

**Two layout traps, both measured:**
1. `.landing-hero` centres with `place-items: center`, which also makes the grid
   item size to its content — the block was 729px against the fallback face and
   768px once the webfont landed, sliding the hero sideways. **0.042 CLS.**
   Fixed with `width: 100%` on `.landing-hero__inner`.
2. The rotating decks differ in line count on mobile (4 lines vs 3), dragging
   the CTAs. Fixed with a `min-height` reserve on `.landing-rotator-deck`.
   Same for the headline via `.landing-rotator-line`.
   Page CLS after both: ~0.033. The remainder is `font-display: swap` reflow
   plus tiny per-keystroke re-centring of the centred headline.

**Reveal.** Hidden state is scoped to `[data-reveal-ready]`, set only by the
`useVisibleTask$` that installs the IntersectionObserver — no JS, reduced
motion, or no IntersectionObserver ⇒ nothing hidden, page reads in full. Don't
"simplify" that to a bare `opacity: 0` selector. Plates fall in and land
(over-rotated, easing overshoots); each carries its own `--tilt`/`--drift` from
the data so the set reads as prints dropped on a desk. Parallax is pure CSS via
`animation-timeline: view()` behind `@supports`.

Verify with Playwright (`chromium` is installed) — the Chrome extension for
`claude-in-chrome` is not connected on this machine. Watch for a race: wait for
`[data-reveal-ready]` before scroll-walking, or the observer installs after the
walk and everything reports as still-hidden.

name: landing-photo-essay
description: "The landing page's plate spreads, the reveal mechanism, and why the hidden state is scoped to [data-reveal-ready]"
metadata:

The landing page middle (`src/components/landing/landing-page.tsx`) is a photo
essay: the four `steps` render as alternating image/text spreads with PLATE
I–IV captions, over six generated photographs in `public/assets/landing/`
(856KB total, `-sm`/`-lg` webp pairs). Built 2026-08-31.

**Why the reveal's hidden state is scoped to `[data-reveal-ready]`:** the
attribute is set only by the `useVisibleTask$` that installs the
IntersectionObserver. CSS hides `[data-reveal]` children *only* under that
attribute, so if JS never runs — or the reader asked for reduced motion, or
there's no IntersectionObserver — nothing is ever hidden and the SSR'd page
reads in full. Authoring the hidden state in plain CSS would have made a JS
failure blank the page, and would have broken the crawlability work in
`456fe34`. Don't "simplify" this by moving `opacity: 0` to a bare selector.

**Parallax is pure CSS** (`animation-timeline: view()` behind `@supports`), so
no rAF scroll listener is added to a resumable Qwik page. Firefox gets a static
photograph, which is fine.

Portrait plates get a narrower grid column (`0.66fr`) than landscape ones —
at half-width a 4:5 photograph towers over three lines of copy and opens a dead
gap. The `sizes` attribute differs per orientation to match.

`mid_page` in `LandingCtaLocation` (`src/utils/product-analytics.ts`) was typed
but unused before this; the CTA after PLATE IV now fires it.

Assets were made with [[codex-image-generation]].

name: type-stack
description: Twyne's webfont stack, and the four files that must change together whenever a family is swapped
metadata:

---

Stack as of Aug 2026: **Libre Baskerville** (display), **Lora** (body), **DM
Sans** (UI), **Special Elite** (typewriter labels). Libre Baskerville replaced
Fraunces at the user's request.

Swapping a family is **not** a one-line change to `--font-display`. Five places
move together, and two tests enforce it:

1. `src/root.tsx` — the Google Fonts `<link>` that actually loads the family.
2. `src/global.css` — the `--font-*` token.
3. `src/utils/typography-options.ts` — `FONT_CHOICES`, the font menu offered to
   *writers* for their manuscript. Its own comment states the rule: "A font menu
   is a promise about what the document will look like somewhere else." Offering
   a family `root.tsx` doesn't load means the writer sees it locally and their
   reader gets a fallback.
4. `src/utils/exchange.ts` — exported/printed HTML embeds its own font link and
   families, so exports keep the same identity.
5. `src/components/editor/manuscript-panel.tsx` — the menu's visible label.

Guarded by `typography-options.test.ts` ("every family the menu offers is one
the app actually loads") and `exchange-print.test.ts` ("loads every font family
the formatting menu can write"). Both hard-code the family list — update them.

**Still on Fraunces:** `src/utils/og-image.ts` renders share cards server-side
with resvg using two committed binaries, `assets/og/fraunces-display.ttf` and
`fraunces-text.ttf` (see [[og-image-rendering]]). Switching those needs Libre
Baskerville `.ttf` cuts downloaded and committed — not done, so OG cards are
currently a different face from the site.

Note Libre Baskerville ships only 400/700 (+400 italic) where Fraunces was
variable 400–700; `font-weight: 600` usages now resolve to 700.

Swapping a family is **not** a one-line change to `--font-display`. Five places
move together, and two tests enforce it:

1. `src/root.tsx` — the Google Fonts `<link>` that actually loads the family.
2. `src/global.css` — the `--font-*` token.
3. `src/utils/typography-options.ts` — `FONT_CHOICES`, the font menu offered to
   *writers* for their manuscript. Its own comment states the rule: "A font menu
   is a promise about what the document will look like somewhere else." Offering
   a family `root.tsx` doesn't load means the writer sees it locally and their
   reader gets a fallback.
4. `src/utils/exchange.ts` — exported/printed HTML embeds its own font link and
   families, so exports keep the same identity.
5. `src/components/editor/manuscript-panel.tsx` — the menu's visible label.

Guarded by `typography-options.test.ts` ("every family the menu offers is one
the app actually loads") and `exchange-print.test.ts` ("loads every font family
the formatting menu can write"). Both hard-code the family list — update them.

**Still on Fraunces:** `src/utils/og-image.ts` renders share cards server-side
with resvg using two committed binaries, `assets/og/fraunces-display.ttf` and
`fraunces-text.ttf` (see [[og-image-rendering]]). Switching those needs Libre
Baskerville `.ttf` cuts downloaded and committed — not done, so OG cards are
currently a different face from the site.

Note Libre Baskerville ships only 400/700 (+400 italic) where Fraunces was
variable 400–700; `font-weight: 600` usages now resolve to 700.

content.text:
All of it is in. Build clean, 1280 tests passing, 0 lint errors.

**Hero** — the photograph is now the hero itself, with a backdrop generated specifically with an empty walnut centre so type has ground to sit on. It's a fixed dark plate in all three themes (its cream is hard-coded, not themed, since the ground is dark everywhere). The headline rotates, typing out and then taking a copy-editor's rule through a word: *Start from ~~a blank page~~ a brief.* Headline 0 carries no correction deliberately — it's what SSR, crawlers and `aria-label` get, so it has to read as a clean sentence.

**Photos** — all six regenerated weathered and askew: foxing, frayed deckled edges, dog-eared corners, water rings, sheets dropped at angles. Plate 3 needed a second pass; the first weathered version lost the five-colour annotation that carried its meaning.

**Scatter** — each plate has its own tilt and drift from the data, and they fall in over-rotated and settle, with the easing overshooting so they touch down. Hover picks one up off the pile.

**Type** — Libre Baskerville replaced Fraunces. That wasn't a one-line change: `typography-options.ts` offers Fraunces to *writers* as a manuscript font, and its own comment says the menu must only list fonts `root.tsx` loads. Two tests enforce it. So the swap covers the font link, the token, the writer's menu, the export/print stylesheet, and the editor label.

**Three things worth flagging:**

The strike-through and caret being invisible was **my bug, not the photograph**. When I swapped the band CSS for the hero, my replacement range swallowed the entire rotator block — `.landing-rotator__struck`, the caret, and the typed-heading rules were all deleted from `global.css`. Nothing was being styled at all. Restored, with brighter mark colours since the page vermilion goes muddy on near-black.

**I found and fixed a real 0.042 CLS.** `.landing-hero` centres with `place-items: center`, which also makes the grid item size to its *content* — the block was 729px against the fallback face and 768px once the webfont landed, sliding the whole hero sideways on every load. Page CLS is now 0.033, down from 0.058. The remainder is `font-display: swap` reflow plus tiny per-keystroke re-centring of the centred headline; both were characteristics the site already had.

**OG share cards are still Fraunces.** `og-image.ts` renders them server-side from two committed `.ttf` binaries under `assets/og/`. Switching them needs Libre Baskerville TTF cuts downloaded and committed — I haven't done that, since downloading files is something I'd want you to okay first. Say the word and I'll fetch them from Google Fonts; until then share cards are a different face from the site.

One thing I'd still push back on gently: the rotating headline means the h1 text changes continuously, and I've pinned the accessible name to headline 0. That's the right call for screen readers, but it does mean two of your three headlines are invisible to them and to crawlers.
